newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cypriot finance minister urges spending curbs.
newsitem.headline: Cypriot finance minister urges spending curbs.

text.p: Cyprus's Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou on Thursday urged Cypriots to curb free-spending lifestyles and tighten their belts if they wanted the island's economy to remain healthy.

"We can't have everything from the state without giving as well -- so as not to deprive ourselves of waste, over consumption and insatiable exhibitionism," Christodoulou said with a touch of sarcasm during his annual budget speech to parliament.

With low unemployment and inflation levels which have not exceeded three percent in years, the island has a robust economy but officials have expressed concerns of late that free-spending habits could spur inflation and widen trade deficits.

"We have to list our priorities and get rid of the mentality to easily adopt every demand at the expense of public revenue and the limited resources of national economy," said the minister, known for his bluntness.
The budget, which was tabled to the House in September, forecast a deficit increase of almost 14 percent higher than projected figures for 1996.
The fiscal deficit is expected to reach 175 million pounds ($371.8 million) in 1997 -- 4 percent of gross domestic product -- compared with a deficit of 120 million in 1996, he said.
Nominal GDP growth will reach 3.5 percent in 1997 from 2.5 expected this year. Unemployment is expected to be 2.9 percent, a slight drop from this year's expectation of 3.0 percent.
Inflation in 1997 is expected at 2.8 percent compared to 3.0 percent this year.
The prospective EU member has launched a drive to harmonise its economy with that of the trade bloc, with which it hopes to start accession talks in early to mid-1998.

Cyprus has made deregulation of its monetary sectors, a drive to ease foreign investments and efforts to boost productivity in all sectors the cornerstone of its economic policies in 1997, Christodoulou said.
He said restrictions on foreign exchange movement would be restricted gradually along with the abolition of interest rate ceilings, currently set by law at nine percent.
Opposition left-wing parties oppose deregulating interest rates, fearing they will be pushed up by local banks.
"There will be a dialogue and communication with all those concerned to achieve the maximum possible understanding and acceptance of this unavoidable modernisation," Christodoulou said.

Net spending next year is forecast at 1.48 billion pounds against revenue of 1.09 billion, yeilding a deficit of 388.8 million pounds. Projected spending for 1996 is 1.35 billion pounds against revenue of 1.01 billion, giving a deficit of 341.7 million pounds.

The 1997 budget does not contain any provisions for major tax increases, though last month the government sent legislation to parliament seeking a one percentage point increase of a defence levy on income to three percent from two percent.
A budget for defence spending, treated separately from other budgets, was tabled to the House earlier Thursday. Defence officials refused to release any details.

The budgets do not cover the north of the island which has been occupied by Turkey since an invasion in 1974 sparked by a short lived coup in Nicosia engineered by the military ruling in Greece at the time.
